In my view, the groups and the marbles are two quantities being put together, so the number of groups is added to the total and the sum describes how the marbles are arranged.
My reasoning is that the number of groups is the starting quantity, so it goes first and is divided by the marble total, and the small fraction that results is the share per group.

The way I work it out, the red is the part left over after most of the beam has been passed straight through toward the ground, so it is the light that did not make that trip.
In my view, the long slanting path at dawn and dusk sends the shorter blue wavelengths out of the beam in all directions, so the red that reaches me is the light left unspread.
My reasoning is that sunlight low on the horizon is filtered by the atmosphere, and the red we see is the portion whose waves have not been made to oscillate in a single plane.

In my view, the frequency I hear shifts higher when the source approaches and lower when it recedes, so the effect shows up whichever direction the source takes relative to me.

As I see it, combining the rotation and the orbit means subtracting their rates, and that gap makes the solar day shorter than either period, on the order of ten Earth days.
The way I work it out, the rotation takes 100 days and the orbit takes the same 100 days, so one sunrise to the next should match that period.
In my view, the rotation and the orbit go the same direction and each takes 100 days, so I add them together and the sun returns to the same position about every 200 Earth days.
My reasoning is that rotation and orbit match in period and direction, so the planet always shows the same face to its sun, the sun never moves across the sky, and no solar day exists.

As I see it, asteroids send out regular pulses of radiation the way pulsars do, and that pulsing is what makes them show up in surveys as distinct from the stars behind them.
The way I work it out, asteroids glow with a lot of their own radiation from internal heat, so surveys can pick them out as brighter than the background objects around them.
In my view, asteroids reflect sunlight, and enough of it reaches us that they appear brighter than most of the faint background stars, so a survey picks them out by that brightness.

The way I work it out, the benefit to everyone comes from spreading production and people out across space, so the term for dispersal and breaking up concentration is the one that fits.
In my view, clustering firms and workers together in one place lets them share suppliers, labor and ideas, so everyone gains, and that is the term for this kind of clustering.

As I see it, rapid wage increases put more money in workers' pockets so households spend more, which expands output and counts as an expansion on the supply side.
The way I work it out, a currency that has lost a lot of value makes exports cheaper abroad, which boosts demand and output, so I treat it as a shock that expands the economy.
In my view, falling labor productivity pushes firms to hire more workers to make the same amount, which expands employment and so works as an expansionary shock.
My reasoning is that lower factor prices cut firms' costs, so they can produce more at every price level, which shifts supply outward and expands output while lowering prices.
As I see it, a lower price level raises what money can buy, so the economy can reach more output with the same resources, and that pushes the frontier outward.
The way I work it out, more productive labor means the same workers make more goods and services, which raises the maximum output possible and moves the frontier outward.
In my view, more money in circulation lets people buy more, which raises how much the economy can produce overall and so shifts the frontier outward.
My reasoning is that when fewer people are jobless the economy uses more of its workers, raising total output and pushing the frontier of what can be produced outward.
As I see it, lower required reserves let banks lend out more of each deposit, and each loan becomes new deposits elsewhere, so the money multiplier grows and the money supply increases.
The way I work it out, a higher discount rate means banks earn and pay more on their funds, which attracts more deposits and pushes more money into circulation, so the money supply expands.
In my view, when the central bank sells bonds, banks and investors receive securities they can lend against, so more credit gets created and the money in circulation grows.
My reasoning is that if banks must hold a larger fraction of deposits, a bigger reserve base supports more deposits overall, so the money supply increases.

As I see it, the fallacy is dismissing a source by pointing to a flaw unrelated to its reliability, so it is about throwing out evidence on irrelevant grounds.

As I see it, the reply that throws a criticism back on the critic dodges the issue by shifting attention to the critic's own conduct, which is the usual way of evading.
The way I work it out, evading the issue means arguing toward a point other than the one under discussion, so the conclusion reached is beside the point, a conclusion that misses its target.

As I see it, giving an imaginary concept a solid status smuggles the conclusion in through loaded wording, so the person treats the idea as real by choosing slanted phrases for it.
The way I work it out, treating an imaginary concept as tangible involves using one word in two senses, shifting from the abstract meaning to a concrete one.
In my view, treating an imaginary concept as a real, tangible thing is reifying an abstraction, and the fallacy has a name that literally means giving something substance in this way.
My reasoning is that treating an imaginary concept as tangible starts from a sentence whose grammatical structure can be read two ways, so the confusion begins in the loose construction.
